HediffDef.label: tetanus
HediffDef.description: Lockjaw: a toxin made by bacteria from soil, dung and rust that got into a deep wound left untended. It shows days to a week after the wound as a stiff jaw, then rigid muscles and painful spasms that can stop the breathing. The body builds no lasting immunity to it. Treatment buys time while the toxin wears off over two or three weeks: tending as often as possible, a quiet room, and the best medicine there is. Modern medicine (an antitoxin and antibiotics) makes the greatest difference. Untreated, it often kills. Wounds cleaned and dressed within a few hours don't cause it.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has tetanus. A wound from some days ago wasn't cleaned in time, and the toxin has reached the muscles: the jaw is locking, and the spasms will follow.\n\nUntreated, tetanus can kill within a week. With steady tending the toxin wears off over two or three weeks.

notes.li: Tend the patient often and keep them still and quiet. The best medicine we have goes to this one.

[lowtech] A dark, quiet room, since noise and light set off the spasms. Clean the wound out again, willow bark for the pain, and tend as often as we can. Herbs only slow it; it has to wear off by itself.

[!lowtech] Tetanus antitoxin and antibiotics, now, and the wound cleaned out again. Something for the spasms. Industrial medicine or better makes all the difference. Expect weeks before the stiffness goes.

HediffDef.label: pneumonia
HediffDef.description: An infection deep in the lungs, usually after a cold, a chest cold or the flu, and most dangerous to the old, the frail, small children and the starving. A high fever, chest pain and labored breathing over several days, then the crisis: the fever breaks, or the lungs fail. Bed rest, warmth, food and steady tending carry the patient through, and modern medicine (antibiotics) works far better than herbs. Even after the fever breaks, weakness and a cough linger for a week or two.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef}'s cold has gone to the chest. It's pneumonia: a high fever, pain with every breath, and lungs filling with fluid.\n\nWithout care it can kill in four or five days, sooner in someone old or weak. With bed rest and steady tending, the fever should break within a week.

notes.li: Bed, warmth, food and fluids, and tend the patient as often as we can. Sit them up so they can breathe.
[lowtech] Keep the fire going and the patient propped up. Willow bark for the fever. It comes to a crisis around the fifth day; after that, the fever breaks or it doesn't.
[!lowtech] Antibiotics, as soon as we can. With industrial medicine this is usually a week in bed. Without it, it's a coin toss for the old ones.

HediffDef.label: tuberculosis
HediffDef.description: Consumption: a slow bacterial infection of the lungs, spread through the air to people who sleep in the same room as someone coughing. Weeks after catching it comes a cough that won't go away, night sweats, tiredness and a hunger food never satisfies, and over the months it wastes the body. The cure is a long course of treatment, tended every day for weeks: progress builds only while treatment continues and slips back if it stops early. Modern medicine (a course of antibiotics) works far better than herbs; before it, rest, good food and fresh air were all anyone had. A sick colonist in a room of their own stops it spreading.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has a cough that won't go away, night sweats and no appetite. It's tuberculosis, caught weeks ago from someone sharing the same room.\n\nIt's slow: untreated, it wastes a person over a month or two. The cure takes daily treatment for weeks, and the sick should sleep apart from everyone else so it goes no further.

notes.li: A room of their own, and treatment every day, without gaps, for as long as it takes. Stopping early lets it come back.
[lowtech] Rest, fresh air, the best food we have, and a bed by an open window. Herbs ease the cough. It's a long road; some walk it, some don't.
[!lowtech] A daily course of antibiotics from the medicine shelf, for weeks, and industrial medicine at least. Keep the patient apart until the cough has gone.

HediffDef.label: typhus
HediffDef.description: Epidemic typhus, carried by body lice in crowded, dirty sleeping quarters. About a week after the bite comes a sudden high fever and a pounding headache, then a rash spreading from the chest, and in bad cases stupor and delirium. Untreated it often kills; with good tending most recover, and modern medicine (antibiotics) clears it fast. Clean rooms, washing and fewer people to a room stop the lice, and with them the spread. Children have a milder course.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has typhus. Lice from the crowded, dirty sleeping quarters carried it, and now there's a high fever and a pounding headache. A rash will follow.\n\nUntreated, typhus can kill within a week. With steady tending most recover. Clean the room and keep the patient apart, or the lice will carry it to the others.

notes.li: Wash the patient, burn the bedding and scrub that room. Then tend the fever as often as we can.
[lowtech] Boil the clothes and blankets, cut the hair short, and keep the fever down with cool cloths and willow bark. A clean bed in a clean room.
[!lowtech] Antibiotics clear it in a few days, so industrial medicine is the thing here. Delouse everyone who slept in that room.

HediffDef.label: meningitis
HediffDef.description: A bacterial infection of the lining around the brain and spine. It comes on suddenly: fever, a crushing headache, a stiff neck and pain from bright light, then confusion and seizures. It moves within hours and kills within two days without treatment. Tend the patient at once and as often as possible; modern medicine (antibiotics, given quickly) is what saves most people, and a skilled doctor matters more here than anywhere. Survivors are weak for a while afterward.

notes.li: Every hour counts. Tend now, then again the moment the last treatment wears off. A dark room and cool cloths.
[lowtech] Keep the room dark and quiet and the fever down. Herbs alone may not be enough, so whoever has the steadiest hands should tend this one, day and night.
[!lowtech] Antibiotics immediately, the best we have, glitterworld medicine if there is any. The first day decides it.

HediffDef.label: scurvy
HediffDef.description: A sickness of the diet, from weeks without fruit or vegetables, raw or cooked into meals. First comes tiredness, then sore gums and aching joints, then bleeding gums, bruises from nothing and wounds that heal slowly and bleed easily. It worsens slowly as long as the diet stays the same, and left for many weeks it kills. The cure is fresh food: once they eat fruit or vegetables again, it clears within a couple of weeks. Medicine does nothing for it.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has scurvy. There hasn't been a fruit or a vegetable on {PAWN_nameDef}'s plate in weeks, and it shows: tiredness first, and soon sore gums and aching joints.\n\nIt worsens slowly as long as the diet stays the same, and can kill if left for many weeks. Fruit or vegetables, raw or in meals, will cure it within a couple of weeks.

notes.li: Fruit or vegetables, at every meal if we can. Nothing else will fix it, and medicine won't help.
[lowtech] Berries, greens, roots, anything that grew. Cooked into a stew is fine.
[!lowtech] It's vitamin C. Fruit and vegetables, raw or cooked; survival meals and meat alone won't do it.

HediffDef.label: glassblood
HediffDef.description: A fever from a crystalline spore that lives in the dust of ancient structures, breathed in by people breaking into ruins, opening old caskets or hauling ancient junk. A day or two later comes the fever, and a faint glitter along the veins; then the joints stiffen as if turning to glass. Untreated, it can stop the heart and lungs within a week. Steady tending keeps the fever down while the body clears the spores, and herbs help nearly as much as modern medicine. Survivors are weak for a while.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has a fever, and there's a faint glitter along the veins of both arms. It's glassblood, from spores in the dust of the ancient ruins.\n\nUntreated, the joints stiffen and the fever can stop the heart within a week. With steady tending most recover. Whoever goes back into those ruins shouldn't stay long.

notes.li: Keep the fever down and tend the patient as often as we can. Herbs do nearly as well as anything for this one.
[lowtech] Cool cloths, willow bark and warm water for the joints. The old stories say the glitter fades when the fever does.
[!lowtech] The scanner shows the spores in the blood. Fever control and steady tending; antibiotics barely touch it.

HediffDef.label: cholera
HediffDef.description: A bacterial infection of the gut, spread through water and food fouled by the sick: in hot weather, in crowded and dirty quarters, or from a cook who didn't wash. Half a day to two days after catching it come watery diarrhea and vomiting so heavy that the body dries out within hours. Untreated it can kill in two or three days. The cure is rehydration: water with a little salt and sugar, sip by sip, as often as the patient can take it, so steady tending matters far more than the kind of medicine. Modern medicine (fluids and antibiotics) shortens it further. It passes to people who sleep in the same dirty room; clean water, clean hands and clean rooms stop it.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has cholera: watery diarrhea and vomiting that won't stop, and {PAWN_pronoun} is drying out by the hour. It came from fouled water or food, or from someone else who has it.\n\nUntreated, cholera can kill in two or three days. Kept drinking and tended steadily, most people are over it within a week. Clean the room {PAWN_nameDef} sleeps in, or it will spread.

notes.li: Water, a little salt and a little sugar, a cup at a time, day and night. That's what saves them, more than any medicine. Then scrub everything.
[lowtech] Boil all the water, and keep the sick away from the kitchen and the well. Salted water with honey, sip by sip, and someone sitting with them all night.
[!lowtech] Oral rehydration salts, or a drip if they can't keep it down, and antibiotics. Boil the water and disinfect the latrine and that room.

HediffDef.label: appendicitis
HediffDef.description: An inflamed appendix: a pain that starts around the navel and settles low on the right side of the belly, with fever, sickness and no appetite. Over a day or two it worsens, and if the appendix bursts, the infection spreads through the belly and can kill within days. The sure cure is surgery to take it out, which any doctor with medicine and a steady hand can do (the "remove appendix" operation). Without surgery, steady tending gives the body a chance to wall the infection off: modern antibiotics often calm it on their own, while with herbs alone it's a close thing. It never comes back once the appendix is out, or after the body has fought it off.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has a pain low on the right side of the belly that's getting worse by the hour, with a fever and no appetite. It's appendicitis.\n\nIf the appendix bursts, the infection spreads and can kill within days. The sure cure is to take it out: a doctor can do the "remove appendix" operation with two medicine. Until then, or with no surgeon to do it, tend {PAWN_nameDef} as often as possible.

notes.li: It has to come out, and the sooner the better. I'll need clean hands, good light and two doses of medicine.
[lowtech] Cut it out, quickly and cleanly, before it bursts. If no one can, cold packs on the belly, nothing to eat and willow bark, and hope it walls itself off.
[!lowtech] Antibiotics straight away, and surgery as soon as we can manage it. A burst appendix is a much harder operation.

HediffDef.label: rabies
HediffDef.description: A virus passed in the bite of a sick animal. For a week or two nothing shows but the bite itself. Then come fever and a tingling at the wound, then agitation, a terror of water and paralysis, and once those symptoms show it is fatal within days, whatever anyone does. Before then it can be stopped: the bite washed out, and treatment kept up every day until the danger has passed. Modern medicine (the vaccine and antibodies) does it in days; with herbs and wound care alone it takes weeks of tending without a break. A bite cleaned and dressed within a few hours is half as likely to pass it on.

li.letterText: The animal that bit {PAWN_nameDef} wasn't right: foam at the mouth, no fear, biting at anything. {PAWN_nameDef} may have rabies.\n\nNothing shows yet, and there is time. Treatment every day from now until the danger has passed will stop it; modern medicine works fastest. If the treatment lapses and the fever and the fear of water come, nothing will save {PAWN_objective}.

notes.li: Wash the bite out, long and hard, and treat it every single day. We don't stop until I say so.
[lowtech] Wash it with soap and running water until your arms ache, then burn it clean. Treat it every day for weeks. There's no second chance with this one.
[!lowtech] The vaccine course and antibodies into the wound, starting today. Industrial medicine or better. Done properly, this one is beaten.

HediffDef.label: measles
HediffDef.description: A very catching childhood fever. About a week after catching it come a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and red eyes, then a blotchy rash that spreads from the face downward. The sickest days are around the rash; most children are over it in ten days or so, weak for a while after. Nothing cures it: rest, fluids, a dim room for sore eyes and someone keeping watch. It passes to any child who shares the room and hasn't had it. The grown-ups had it long ago, and a child who has had measles never gets it again.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has measles: a high fever, a cough and red, sore eyes, and the rash will follow in a day or two. It's very catching.\n\nMost children are over it in ten days or so with rest, fluids and someone to keep watch. Any child who shares {PAWN_possessive} room and hasn't had it may catch it too.

notes.li: Bed, plenty to drink, the curtains drawn for the eyes, and someone to sit with them. Keep the other children out of that room.
[lowtech] Cool cloths for the fever and broth when they'll take it. Keep the room dim. The other children sleep elsewhere until the rash fades.
[!lowtech] Fever medicine, fluids and vitamin A. Watch for labored breathing. Children who haven't had it sleep apart.

HediffDef.label: kidney stone
HediffDef.description: A small stone of salts formed in the kidney, now working its way out. It brings waves of terrible pain in the side and back, sickness, and blood in the urine. It's one of the worst pains there is, but it isn't dangerous: most stones pass on their own within a week. Plenty to drink, warmth and something for the pain help it along, and modern medicine eases the passage. Hot weather and too little to drink make stones likelier.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} is doubled up with pain in the side and back, coming in waves, and has been sick twice. It's a kidney stone.\n\nIt isn't dangerous, and most stones pass on their own within a week, but the pain is terrible. Plenty to drink and a doctor to ease the pain will help it along.

notes.li: Water, and more water. Something for the pain, a hot cloth on the back, and patience. It will pass.
[lowtech] Warm baths, a hot stone on the back and plenty of weak tea. Poppy for the worst of the pain, if we have any.
[!lowtech] Strong painkillers, fluids, and a muscle relaxant to help it through. Strain the urine so we know when it's out.

HediffDef.label: shingles
HediffDef.description: The chickenpox virus, asleep in the nerves since childhood, waking again in someone older: first a burning or tingling on one side of the body, then a band of painful blisters along it. It heals over two or three weeks and isn't dangerous, but the pain can be fierce, and in some it lingers as nerve pain after the rash is gone. Rest, cool cloths and something for the pain help; modern medicine (an antiviral, started early) shortens it a good deal. It comes to people of fifty and older.

li.letterText: {PAWN_nameDef} has a band of red blisters around one side of {PAWN_possessive} ribs, and says it burns like fire. It's shingles: the old chickenpox, back after all these years.\n\nIt isn't dangerous and heals in two or three weeks, but it's painful. Treatment eases it, and modern medicine shortens it.

notes.li: Loose clothes, cool cloths and rest. Something for the pain at night so they can sleep.
[lowtech] Cool compresses, a paste of oats, and willow bark for the pain. Keep it clean and covered, and don't let anyone burst the blisters.
[!lowtech] Antivirals, the sooner the better, and proper painkillers. Keep the blisters covered around the children.

HediffDef.label: hive fever
HediffDef.description: A fever from the bites and stings of insectoids, which carry something in their saliva the body has never met. A day after the wound it swells and goes hot; then comes the fever, in bad cases a low hum in the ears that won't stop and growing confusion, and at the end convulsions. Untreated it can kill within a week. Steady tending keeps the fever down while the body learns to fight it, and modern medicine helps more than herbs. Survivors are weak for a while.

li.letterText: The insect wound on {PAWN_nameDef} has swollen up hot and hard, and now there's a fever. {PAWN_nameDef} says there's a humming in {PAWN_possessive} ears. It's hive fever, from the insectoids' saliva.\n\nUntreated, it can kill within a week. With steady tending most recover, and modern medicine works better than herbs.

notes.li: Keep the fever down and the wound clean, and tend the patient as often as we can. Talk to them when the humming gets bad.
[lowtech] Open the wound and draw the poison with a hot poultice, cool cloths for the fever, and willow bark. Someone stays with them at night.
[!lowtech] Antivenom isn't made for these things, so it's antibiotics, fever control and fluids. Clean the hive's leavings out of the tunnels.

RecipeDef.label: remove appendix
RecipeDef.description: Remove an inflamed appendix before it bursts. It cures appendicitis at once; the patient needs some days to get their strength back afterward.
